newsitem.title: LEBANON: Bekaa Valley has a history as Lebanon's wild west.
newsitem.headline: Bekaa Valley has a history as Lebanon's wild west.

text.p: The lush greenery of eastern Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, wedged between snow-capped mountains, belies its history as the country's wild west and home to some of the world's deadliest guerrilla groups.

The Syrian-controlled valley, where some members of the Japanese Red Army were captured last week, was a hotbed for a mix of armed factions during the 1975-90 civil war, from the Shi'ite Moslem Hizbollah to radical Palestinians and Kurdish Marxists.

The Red Army, which set up base in the Bekaa when it was founded in 1971, had links with radical Palestinian groups which with leftist Lebanese factions were the main presence in the fertile plain up to the early 1980s.

But after Israel invaded in 1982 hundreds of Iranian Revolutionary Guards arrived via Syria to train groups to fight the Israelis, especially Hizbollah guerrillas who ruled supreme in the valley, turning cities like Baalbek into Tehran-style Islamic fiefdoms.

As the Lebanese government began to extend its authority across the country after the end of the 1975-90 civil war, Hizbollah handed over its largest base in Lebanon -- the Sheikh Abdallah barracks at Baalbek -- to the Lebanese army in 1992.
But Hizbollah still maintains a strong presence in the Bekaa, whose dusty villages are recruiting grounds for militants to fight Israeli occupation forces in south Lebanon.

The Sheikh Abdallah barracks overlooking Baalbek's magnificent Roman temples was believed to be one of several places where clandestine Moslem groups believed linked to Hizbollah held Western hostages during the civil war.

It was also headquarters for Iranian Revolutionary Guards, scores of whom are believed to remain in remote areas of the valley that lies between the snow-capped Mount Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges.

Lebanese troops took over in 1992 the main Bekaa training base for the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), where hundreds of fighters were trained each year before crossing into Turkey through Syria to fight for Kurdish independence.
Syria, whose 35,000 troops in Lebanon make it Beirut's main power broker, agreed to crack down on the PKK after Ankara indicated it might bomb the group's bases near the Syria-Lebanon border.
Turkey's urban guerrilla group Dev-Sol (Revolutionary Left) and the Turkish Liberation Army of Workers and Villagers (TIKKO) are also believed to have had bases in the Bekaa in the past.
At least one radical Palestinian faction, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine-General Command (PFLP-GC) still has small bases in the valley.
Last week, Israeli warplanes raided a PFLP-GC base in hills at Sultan Yacoub west of the border with Syria, wounding three guerrillas.
Another feature that made the Bekaa famous for lawlessness was the lucrative drugs trade that thrived there during the war.

Some of the world's choicest hashish -- known as Lebanese Blond -- was grown in the Bekaa in addition to opium poppies from which heroin is extracted. Syrian and Lebanese forces have cracked down on the trade in recent years, and Beirut says the illegal crops have been wiped out.
